title: Kindness and bias
hook: a few weeks of loving-kindness practice reduced one measure of racial bias in one study (Kang, Gray and Dovidio)

segments.voice: Yesterday: trainable. Compassion as a beginning to develop, not a hand you're dealt. Who got your quiet wish? Day one thousand three hundred seven.

Some reactions arrive before any thought does. A face on a train, a voice on the phone, an accent at the counter, and something in the body leans in or leans away a split second before the mind has a say. Psychologists have built tests to catch those split seconds, and what they catch can be uncomfortable: quiet leanings people would never choose and might never admit. Yesterday said compassion can be trained. Today asks a sharper question. Can a practice of goodwill reach down into those split seconds too?
screen: `A FACE ON A TRAIN.` → `THE BODY LEANS FIRST.` → `CAN GOODWILL REACH THAT DEEP?`

segments.voice: First, the practice. Loving-kindness, in Pali metta, comes from Buddhist teaching. A short discourse called the Metta Sutta describes it: wishing that all beings be happy and at ease, whether weak or strong, near or far, seen or unseen, and holding that goodwill toward the whole world the way a mother guards her only child. Second, the study. Psychologists Yoona Kang, Jeremy Gray and John Dovidio gave a group of non-Black adults a short course in loving-kindness practice over a few weeks. A second group learned about loving-kindness and discussed it, but didn't practice it. A third group simply waited. Third, the measure. Afterward, everyone took a timed computer test of automatic associations, the kind that catches the split-second leanings. In this study, the group that actually practiced loving-kindness showed less automatic bias toward Black people, and toward homeless people too. The group that only talked about it did not. Fourth, honesty about the size of it. This was one study, one kind of test, a modest group of people. Those split-second tests are debated among psychologists, and nobody showed that a few weeks of practice rewrote anyone's whole outlook. So the careful claim is small: in this study, practicing goodwill, not just discussing it, moved one measure in a fairer direction. In this study, information alone didn't move it. Practice did: wishing well, again and again, toward a circle that keeps getting wider.
screen: `METTA: GOODWILL TO ALL BEINGS.` · `PRACTICE, TALK, OR WAIT.` · then, large: `ONLY PRACTICE MOVED THE MEASURE.` · then: `ONE STUDY, HONESTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish someone unlike you well. Sit and settle. Bring to mind someone you love, and hold one simple wish for them: may you be happy, may you be at ease. Then bring to mind a person who seems very unlike you, in age, in background, in how they live. A face from the bus, the checkout line or the news. Offer them the same wish, with the same warmth, as if they were just as near. Notice whatever arises, and keep wishing. The bell holds the time.
Kindness and bias. In one study, practicing loving-kindness, not just discussing it, lowered one measure of automatic bias. Today's word.
Your line: wider. Today, when you notice yourself leaning away from someone, add them to the circle with one quiet wish for their good. Day one thousand three hundred seven.

howItsDone: In Buddhist loving-kindness (metta) practice, people repeat simple wishes for well-being, starting with themselves or a loved one and widening step by step to strangers, difficult people and all beings, as the Metta Sutta describes.

what a scholar hears: the result rests on an implicit association test, a measure psychologists still debate, so it's a promising single finding, not a settled one.
